memo_script:
da — quick one. no homework in this one, just something I want you to have in your ear before the trip.

There's a little word the aunties run on. Everything they know, they heard from someone, who heard it from someone else. And Tamil has a tag for exactly that — the hearsay tag.

-ஆம்.

You stick it on the end. வராங்கலாம் — apparently they're coming. சாப்பிட்டாங்களாம் — apparently they ate. ஊர்ல இல்லையாம் — apparently he's not in town.

You don't need to fire it. You just need to catch it — because it's going to be everywhere at that table. Every piece of gossip that comes at you will be trailing one of these. Once you hear it once, you'll hear it in everything.

அந்த -ஆம் — that's the sound of someone passing along what they heard. The aunties live in that register.

That's it. Just let it soak. see you soon.

body: 🎧 you asked for a soak — here's the gauntlet, full speed. three lines, one landing.
memo_script:
Picture the moment.

You've just walked through the front door. Bags down. And before you can even breathe, an aunty materialises — the fast kind, the one who asks three questions before you've answered the first.

She hits you with: "Evlo naal irupeenga?"

And you don't hesitate. You say it clean:

ஒரு மாசம் இருப்போம்.

One month, we're staying. That's it. Short, settled, no fumbling. She nods — already moving to the next one.

"Enna velai paakareenga?"

And this is where a lot of people freeze. But not you. You've got:

சாஃப்ட்வேர் இன்ஜினியரா இருக்கேன்.

I'm a software engineer. That's your Oracle-approved form — not any other version, this one. She's already half-impressed, half-figuring out who to tell.

Then she gestures around — at the house, at the family spilling out of the kitchen — and she asks what she actually wants to hear:

"Pidichirukka?"

And you land it:

ரொம்ப பிடிச்சிருக்கு.

I really like it. Not polite. Real. That's the melt line — food, place, people, all of it, one phrase.

Three questions. Three answers. ஒரு மாசம் இருப்போம். சாஃப்ட்வேர் இன்ஜினியரா இருக்கேன். ரொம்ப பிடிச்சிருக்கு.

The gauntlet's yours. Let them run it.

body: 🎙️ 90 seconds on the phrase that melts every auntie — no ask, just the story. worth a listen.
memo_script:
Picture this.

You've just eaten. The plate is clean. The auntie who cooked is watching you from the corner of the room — she's pretending to arrange something on the counter, but she's watching.

In England, you say "that was delicious." Nice. Polite. Forgotten by morning.

In a Coimbatore kitchen, you say: ரொம்ப பிடிச்சிருக்கு.

ரொம்ப — so much, really, deeply. பிடிச்சிருக்கு — it has grabbed me. It has *caught* me and won't let go.

Not "I liked it." Not "it was good." The food reached across the plate and took hold of something in you. That's what you're telling her.

And here's the thing about Tamil aunties and food — cooking is not just cooking. It's years of learning her mother-in-law's hand, the exact ratio of chilli to coriander her family expects, the pride that goes into every pot. When you say ரொம்ப பிடிச்சிருக்கு, you're not reviewing a dish. You're telling her the years landed.

Your wife's family is going to put food in front of you approximately every forty-five minutes. This phrase is your single most powerful tool in that house.

ரொம்ப பிடிச்சிருக்கு. Romba pidichirukku.

Hold that. You'll know exactly when.
